title: Technoference in the Home: Development and Preliminary Feasibility Testing of an Animated Child‐Report Measure
abstract: ABSTRACT Parental technoference is increasingly recognised as a common aspect of contemporary family life, yet no existing measures allow young children to directly report on parental technoference. This study developed and preliminarily tested the Child‐Report Measure of Technoference in the Home, an animated, scenario‐based measure designed to assess parental technoference using children as informants. Across two phases, we (1) reviewed and prioritised existing technoference items with experts and co‐designed animated technoference scenarios with children and (2) conducted pilot testing with 45 children aged 5–9 years. Children demonstrated high engagement and comprehension across animations, and most emotion faces used in the response format were accurately identified. In the pilot, 91% of children reported parental technoference in at least one scenario. Sadness was the most frequently reported emotional response. Younger children (5–6 years) reported higher prevalence and frequency than older children (7–9 years). Boys reported higher frequency in one scenario depicting parent‐initiated technoference. No other age and sex differences were found. These findings indicate that young children can meaningfully engage in the co‐design and testing of developmentally appropriate child‐report measures. Children aged 5.5–9 years were able to use the animated scenarios to report on both the occurrence and perceived emotional impact of parental technoference in the home, demonstrating the feasibility of this measure. Directions for future validation, refinement and broader application in research and practice are discussed.
